events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius: exact onset time (first quote timeout) vs 12:16 report, which services actually show errors/latency degradation between ~11:30 and 13:59 (order-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service, and any shared dependencies), the dominant error signature on quote timeouts (downstream timeout vs serialization/deserialization error), and resource trends (CPU, memory, connection pool, thread saturation) on the quote path. Also determine whether pricing-engine p99 2.6s is elevated vs its baseline and when it started rising.

Enumerate all changes in the window 11:30-13:59 across ALL services, not just market-data-service: deployments (including the market-data-service serialization change), config changes, and feature flags, with exact timestamps and affected services/components. Map the dependency graph of order-service's quote path (what it calls, what pricing-engine and market-data-service depend on, shared components like queues/caches/DBs). Search historical incidents for similar quote-timeout / serialization-change patterns and their confirmed root causes.

Correlate the change list from task b against the onset time found in task a: identify which change (if any) precedes the first degradation, which changes are on the quote path vs unrelated, and whether multiple services degraded simultaneously (pointing to a shared component) or only order-service (pointing to a local cause). Produce a ranked root-cause hypothesis with supporting/contradicting evidence for each candidate.

events.statement: First order-service quote timeout occurred at 2026-05-20T12:06:10Z ("pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms orderId=4bd44879"), about 10 minutes before the 12:16 report. All 225 error logs in the window share the single pattern 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after <n>ms'.

Pricing-engine emitted its first error at 2026-05-20T12:06:41Z — 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' — all 276 errors share this identical pattern; the downstream-error signature is a deadline/timeout, not a (de)serialization failure.

market-data-service logged ZERO errors between 08:00Z and 13:59Z; its only log of any level in this span is a single benign WARN 'deprecated TLS cipher offered by client' at 11:43:53Z. It shows no error/latency symptom despite the report blaming its serialization change.

pricing-engine latency_p99_ms was stable ~59-60ms through 11:58 (11:58 avg 58.97), then jumped to avg 2609.71 / max 2849.25 in the 12:05 bucket and stayed ~2600-2700ms thereafter. Onset is between 11:58 and 12:05, and 2600ms is ~43x the baseline. (420s buckets, so exact minute within 12:05-12:12 is not resolvable at this resolution.)

pricing-engine cpu_pct was ~40% through 11:58 (11:58 avg 39.89), then saturated to avg 99.11-99.33% / max 100% starting in the 12:05 bucket and remained pinned ~99% for the rest of the window — i.e. CPU saturation and the latency jump start in the same 12:05 bucket.

order-service latency_p99_ms rose from ~149-154ms baseline (11:58 avg 150.91) to avg 2433-2972ms in the same 12:05 bucket, tracking the pricing-engine onset; order-service available metrics include db_pool_in_use and restarts (not yet examined).

events.answer: Quote timeouts on order-service began at 12:06:10Z, ~10 minutes before the 12:16 report, and coincide exactly with pricing-engine latency/cpu saturation onset (12:05 bucket). Telemetry shows a pure downstream-timeout signature (2500ms client timeout on order-service; 2000ms deadline exceeded in pricing-engine, calculator=GreeksV2) — no serialization/deserialization errors anywhere. market-data-service logged zero errors, so the reported service is order-service with pricing-engine as the degraded dependency; pricing-engine p99 (~2600ms) is ~43x its ~60ms baseline and started rising between 11:58 and 12:05.

order-service quote path dependency graph: order-service -> pricing-engine (http), -> ledger-db (db), -> exchange-gateway (http), -> kafka (queue-produce); pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http) and -> redis-cache (cache). So order-service's quote does NOT call market-data-service directly -- it goes order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service.

Shared components in the quote path: redis-cache is marked shared:true and is a dependency of BOTH pricing-engine (cache) and market-data-service (cache); ledger-db and kafka are also shared:true. market-data-service additionally calls exchange-gateway (http) and is called by portfolio-service and api-gateway.

These are leads only.

events.answer: In the 11:30-13:59 window there were exactly TWO changes across all services: (1) dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf', deployed 11:56:00Z, still live (not rolled back); and (2) cfg-3120, pricing-engine feature-flag ramp flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 at 12:04:00Z. order-service's quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service, with pricing-engine also hitting redis-cache (a shared cache also used by market-data-service); order-service itself calls pricing-engine, ledger-db, exchange-gateway and kafka. Both the serialization deploy (11:56) and the Greeks-v2 flag ramp (12:04) precede the 12:16Z report, so both are candidate changes, and history offers three matching-lead precedents (HIST-113 CPU/capacity, HIST-107 redis cold-cache, HIST-101 bad deployment).

events.statement: The only code deployment in 11:30-13:59 across ALL services is dep-6111: market-data-service v5.2.0, deployed 2026-05-20T11:56:00Z by v.rao, summary 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf', status 'live', rolled_back_at null. It precedes the first order-service quote timeout (12:06:10Z) by ~10 minutes but is NOT on order-service's direct call path (order-service does not call market-data-service directly; it reaches it only via pricing-engine).

The only config/flag change in the window is cfg-3120 on pricing-engine: flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct changed 5 -> 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by pm-experiments, 'Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'. This timestamp sits BETWEEN the 11:58-12:05 latency/CPU onset bucket and is ~2 minutes before the first order-service quote timeout at 12:06:10Z. Note the pricing-engine error signature explicitly names the ramped calculator: 'calculator=GreeksV2'.

Dependency graph confirms order-service's quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http), with pricing-engine also depending on redis-cache (cache) and market-data-service also depending on redis-cache. So market-data-service is only reachable from order-service transitively through pricing-engine.

redis-cache is a shared:true datastore with multiple upstream consumers (auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service), so it is a plausible shared-component path; however T1 reported no serialization/deserialization errors and the pricing-engine failure mode is CPU saturation (99-100%) on GreeksV2 computation, which a cache miss storm would not by itself explain. A cold-cache storm (HIST-107) would be expected to show cache-miss symptoms, not 100% CPU pinned on the calculator.

Historical precedents for the exact symptom pair ('quote timeouts' + 'cpu 99%' on pricing-engine) exist: HIST-113 (2026-01-28) root cause 'Record market-open volume exceeded provisioned capacity' (capacity_saturation, resolution raised replica count). HIST-107 (2025-12-09) is a shared-redis cold-cache storm with 'quote latency'. HIST-101 (2025-08-14) is a bad_deployment whose symptom included 'high cpu'. These are leads only, not evidence about this incident.

RANKED CANDIDATE ASSESSMENT — (1) cfg-3120 GreeksV2 100% ramp at 12:04 is the leading candidate: it is the only change whose timing aligns with the 11:58->12:05 CPU/latency onset and the 12:06:10 product-visible failure, its owner service is the degraded dependency, and the error names calculator=GreeksV2. Supporting: pricing-engine CPU 40%->99% and p99 60ms->2600ms in the same bucket. (2) dep-6111 protobuf deploy at 11:56 is a weaker candidate: it predates onset by ~8 min and market-data-service shows zero errors (F3), contradicting a serialization defect there; the serialization change would also be expected to produce (de)serialization errors, which T1 found none of. (3) shared redis-cache is a lower-ranked shared-component hypothesis, unsupported so far because no cache-miss/latency signal from market-data-service or auth/portfolio was reported. (4) pure capacity saturation (HIST-113-like) cannot be excluded and would be indistinguishable from the flag ramp on CPU metrics alone.

events.description: The exact minute of the pricing-engine latency/CPU onset is not resolvable: T1's metrics are in 420s buckets, so both cfg-3120 (12:04) and the 12:05 bucket boundary fall inside the same unresolved 11:58->12:05 interval. Deployment/flag timestamps cannot be ordered against the true onset more precisely than 'both precede the first timeout at 12:06:10Z' without a finer metric window.

No metric query was run against redis-cache, ledger-db, kafka or market-data-service to confirm/deny a shared-component (cold cache, DB/queue saturation) contribution; T1 reported no cache/DB symptom but did not enumerate those components' metrics.

events.answer: Two changes exist in the window and both precede the 12:16 report: dep-6111 (market-data-service protobuf serialization, 11:56:00Z, still live/not rolled back) and cfg-3120 (pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100, 12:04:00Z). Degradation is NOT limited to order-service: pricing-engine (the dependency order-service calls) shows the same onset (latency 60ms->2600ms and CPU 40%->99% starting in the 12:05 bucket), so order-service's timeouts are downstream of pricing-engine. The cfg-3120 GreeksV2 ramp at 12:04 aligns most tightly with the 11:58->12:05 onset and the failure signature names calculator=GreeksV2; the 11:56 protobuf deploy is on a different service (market-data-service, which logged zero errors) and is only transitively on the quote path. Leading hypothesis: pricing-engine-side cause triggered around the GreeksV2 100% ramp, with the protobuf deploy as a weaker secondary candidate.
